meta.title: Egyptian Elections
sources: Wikipedia: Egyptian presidential and parliamentary election articles 1923–2025
National Election Authority figures as reported there

presEras.label: Confirmation by plebiscite
presEras.blurb: For half a century Egypt did not elect presidents, it confirmed them. A single candidate nominated by parliament was put to a yes-or-no vote and returned with 90 to 99% approval, six times in a row. Those votes are recorded in this atlas under referendums, not here.

presEras.label: The multi-candidate era
presEras.blurb: A constitutional amendment in 2005 allowed rival candidates for the first time. Mubarak took 88.6% on a turnout of 23%, his nearest challenger was jailed after the count, and the exercise convinced nobody.

presEras.label: Revolution and counter-revolution
presEras.blurb: The only genuinely competitive presidential election in Egyptian history was held in May and June 2012 and won by the Muslim Brotherhood's Mohamed Morsi with 51.7%. He was removed by the army a year later. The 2014 election that followed returned Sisi with 96.9%.

presEras.label: The Sisi presidency
presEras.blurb: Two further elections at 97.1% and 89.6%. Serious challengers have been arrested, withdrawn under pressure or failed to secure nominations; the 2018 runner-up was a Sisi supporter who entered to avoid a single-candidate ballot.

legEras.label: The liberal monarchy
legEras.blurb: Egypt's parliamentary decades, and the only ones in which the outcome was in doubt. The Wafd won every election it was allowed to contest and was dismissed from office by the king or the British each time it did. Between the 1923 constitution and the 1952 coup, no Wafd government completed a term.

legEras.label: One party
legEras.blurb: The monarchy went in 1952 and with it the parties. The National Union and then the Arab Socialist Union were the only permitted vehicles, half the seats were reserved for workers and farmers, and the union with Syria produced two elections for a state that lasted three years.

legEras.label: The National Democratic Party
legEras.blurb: Sadat allowed platforms, then parties, then arrested their leaders. Under Mubarak the NDP took between two-thirds and nine-tenths of the seats at every election for thirty years, with the Muslim Brotherhood contesting as independents when it was allowed to contest at all. The 2010 election, the most nakedly rigged of them, was followed within weeks by Tahrir Square.

legEras.label: After the revolution
legEras.blurb: The 2011–12 election gave Islamist parties around three-quarters of the seats and was annulled by the courts. Since 2015 the chamber has been elected under a system built around individual seats and pro-government lists, and the largest bloc has supported the president.
